claims.text: Q235 steel's corrosion protection across room- and high-temperature regimes is governed by the formation and stability of an oxide layer.
Temperature influences the stability of the oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Corrosive species influence the stability of the protective layer.
A stable oxide layer causes corrosion protection to persist.
Loss of oxide-layer stability causes corrosion protection to fail.
The hypothesis applies at room temperature and at 700–900 °C.
The hypothesis applies in the presence of corrosive species.
Unexposed Q235 steel without a corrosive environment is the proposed baseline.
Varying temperature and corrosive environment while characterizing Q235 steel can test the proposed oxide-layer mechanism.
Oxide-layer thickness and composition are proposed as measurements of the structural mediator.
Corrosion rate and morphology are proposed as outcome measurements.
Finding an unstable or non-protective oxide layer would falsify the hypothesis.
The exact mechanism responsible for persistence or failure of protection is not fully understood.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that protection may fail when the oxide layer is unstable, but the falsification rule treats observation of an unstable or non-protective layer as falsifying the hypothesis. That observation would instead be compatible with the predicted failure branch.
The conditions include both room temperature and 700–900 °C, whereas the boundary specifies only 700–900 °C, leaving the claimed room-temperature applicability inconsistent.

The mediator is specified categorically as a stable oxide layer, yet the hypothesis is also intended to explain failure through loss of layer stability. The mediator should instead be expressed as oxide-layer stability or integrity, with stable and unstable states.
